html:
Gran Colombia was the republic that Simón Bolívar built out of Spain's Viceroyalty of New Granada, covering today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, from 1819 to 1831. Its official name was the Republic of Colombia; historians added "Gran" to tell it apart from the later country.

Bolívar proclaimed it at Angostura in 1819, months after his victory at Boyacá freed Bogotá. A congress at Cúcuta gave it a constitution in 1821, with Bogotá as capital, Bolívar as president and Francisco de Paula Santander as vice-president, who ran the government while Bolívar fought on in the south. Venezuela was won at Carabobo in 1821, Panama joined the same year, and Sucre's victory at Pichincha in 1822 brought in Quito.

The union was too big and too divided. Venezuelan leaders resented rule from Bogotá, and federalists fought centralists. Bolívar made himself dictator in 1828 and survived an attempt to kill him. In 1830 Venezuela and Ecuador broke away, and Bolívar died that December. The rest became the Republic of New Granada in 1831. Gran Colombia stayed the model for later dreams of uniting the Latin American republics.
